Cenchrea
SEN-kree-uh
proper noun (place)
Greek Kenchreai; the eastern seaport of Corinth, on the Saronic Gulf, serving Corinth's trade toward Asia. The site of a church and the home of Phoebe the deaconess.

📖 Biblical Definition

Cenchrea was the eastern harbor of Corinth, a port town on the Saronic Gulf, notable in the New Testament for being the home of a church, the place where the Apostle Paul fulfilled a vow, and the residence of Phoebe, the woman commended to the Romans as a servant of the church there. After his long ministry at Corinth, Paul departed by way of Cenchrea on his return toward Syria; Luke records, "having shorn his head in Cenchrea: for he had a vow" (Acts 18:18), a reference to a Nazarite-style vow Paul had taken, the shaving of the head marking its completion (cf. Num 6). This brief notice shows the apostle to the Gentiles, who taught that believers are free from the ceremonial law, nonetheless observing a personal vow with Jewish associations — a reminder that Christian liberty does not forbid such personal devotions, though it does not require them, and that Paul became "all things to all men" (1 Cor 9:22) without compromising the gospel. Most significantly, Cenchrea was the home church of Phoebe, whom Paul commends at the close of Romans: "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea: That ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also" (Rom 16:1-2). Phoebe, likely the bearer of the epistle to the Romans, is called a "servant" (Greek diakonos) of the Cenchrean church — honored for her service and her succor of many, including Paul himself. Cenchrea thus testifies to the spread of the gospel into the port towns and trade-centers of the Roman world, to the place of devoted women in the service (not the eldership) of the church, and to the warmth of Christian commendation and hospitality that bound the scattered churches together. From the harbor of Cenchrea the gospel and its letters traveled the sea-lanes of the empire, carried by faithful servants like Phoebe.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The eastern seaport of Corinth, home of a church and of Phoebe the servant (diakonos) commended by Paul (Rom 16:1-2); where Paul completed a Nazarite-style vow by shaving his head (Acts 18:18); a witness to the gospel in the port towns and to devoted women in the church's service.

CENCHREA, proper noun. Greek Kenchreai; the eastern seaport of Corinth on the Saronic Gulf.

Where Paul, departing Corinth, shaved his head for a vow he had taken (a Nazarite-style vow; Acts 18:18).

The home church of Phoebe, commended to the Romans as a servant (diakonos) of the church there (Rom 16:1-2).

Phoebe, likely the bearer of the epistle to the Romans, "a succourer of many, and of myself also" (Rom 16:2).

A witness to the gospel in the port towns of the empire and to the place of devoted women in the church's service.

📖 Key Scripture

Acts 18:18 — "And Paul after this tarried there yet a good while, and then took his leave of the brethren, and sailed thence into Syria... having shorn his head in Cenchrea: for he had a vow."

Romans 16:1-2 — "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea: That ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also."

1 Corinthians 9:22 — "To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some."

1 Timothy 2:12 — "But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Cenchrea is corrupted when Paul's vow is read as inconsistency with his gospel of liberty, when Phoebe's commendation is pressed to overturn the male eldership, or when the warmth of Christian hospitality it models is overlooked.

expand to see more

Phoebe-and-the-eldership over-reading. Phoebe is called a "servant" (Greek diakonos) of the church at Cenchrea, and some press this to argue for women in the ordained teaching/governing offices of elder or (ordained, authoritative) deacon. The text honors Phoebe highly — as a servant, a succourer of many, likely the trusted bearer of the epistle to the Romans — but it does not place her in the teaching-and-ruling office that Scripture reserves to qualified men (1 Tim 2:12; 3:1-7). The word diakonos is used broadly of servants and ministers of many kinds; Phoebe's commendation honors her real and valued service without establishing female eldership. The dictionary gladly honors Phoebe and the many women whose service has blessed the church, within the order Scripture sets — an order that exalts, not diminishes, the dignity of women's ministry, while reserving the eldership to men.

Cenchrea has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal points worth recovering are the model of Christian commendation and hospitality, and the honor given to faithful service. Paul commends Phoebe to the Roman church, asking them to receive her and assist her — the warm, practical network of welcome and aid that bound the scattered churches together (cf. 3 John 5-8). The early church moved on the sea-lanes of the empire carried by such commended servants; letters of commendation, hospitality to traveling believers, and mutual assistance were the sinews of the church's unity. Cenchrea, the harbor from which Phoebe likely carried the epistle to the Romans, reminds the church to honor faithful service and to practice the warm hospitality that receives and aids the Lord's servants.

Greek Kenchreai; the eastern seaport of Corinth on the Saronic Gulf

Where Paul shaved his head for a vow (Nazarite-style) as he departed Corinth (Acts 18:18)

The home church of Phoebe, commended to the Romans as a servant (diakonos) of the church (Rom 16:1-2)

Phoebe, likely the bearer of the epistle to the Romans, "a succourer of many, and of myself also" (Rom 16:2)

A witness to the gospel in the port towns and to the honored service of women within the church's order

Usage

"Cenchrea — the eastern port of Corinth, home of Phoebe the servant of the church (Rom 16:1)."

"Paul shaved his head in Cenchrea, for he had a vow (Acts 18:18): Christian liberty permits personal devotions."

"Phoebe, a succourer of many, likely carried the epistle to the Romans from Cenchrea's harbor."
